title: Cache-Control and Security Headers
subtopics: Content security considerations for API responses
learning_outcomes: Explain how cache-control and security headers affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from cache-control to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on cache-control and security headers in http status codes and response headers. You will connect cache-control to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Cache-Control and Security Headers matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying cache-control deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Status codes carry protocol-level meaning; headers and structured bodies add metadata needed by clients. In this lesson, treat “Cache-Control and Security Headers” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.expected_output: The status gives generic protocol meaning; problem details explain the application-specific conflict without exposing internal traces.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Cache-Control”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Expires” and “Cache directives for sensitive data”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating cache-control and security headers as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
